paragraphs.title: The Opening Prophecy and the Defeat at Carchemish

easy.explanation: The prophecy concerns Egypt and its army.
easy.q: Against whom was the prophecy at the beginning of the passage?

easy.explanation: The passage names Pharaohnecho king of Egypt.
easy.q: Who was the king of Egypt mentioned in the passage?

easy.explanation: The battle took place at Carchemish by the river Euphrates.

answers: Order the buckler and shield and prepare its weapons
medium.explanation: The army was told to prepare shields, horses, spears, and armor.
medium.q: What was the army commanded to do before battle?

medium.explanation: They were beaten down, fled quickly, and did not look back.
medium.q: What happened to Egypt's mighty men after the battle began?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes fear on every side of the army.
medium.q: What does the phrase "fear was round about" mean?

answers: Careful preparation followed by retreat and defeat
Lack of preparation followed by victory
challenge.explanation: Although the army prepared for battle, it became frightened and fell.
challenge.q: What is the main contrast between the army's preparation and the battle's result?

answers: The defeat was widespread and included everyone
The army did not take part in the battle
challenge.explanation: Both the swift and the mighty were unable to escape.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the statement that neither the swift nor the mighty would escape?

challenge.explanation: The army fell toward the north by the river Euphrates.
challenge.q: Which geographical detail is repeated in the description of the defeat?

paragraphs.title: The Raging River and the Coalition Army

easy.explanation: Egypt rises like a flood whose waters are moved like rivers.
The Ethiopians and Libyans handle shields, and the Lydians handle bows.
easy.q: Which weapons are mentioned among the assisting peoples?

easy.explanation: Egypt stumbled, fell, and became ashamed among the nations.
easy.q: What was the result of the battle at the end of the passage?

answers: To emphasize its great power and desire to cover the earth
medium.explanation: The image presents Egypt as a force surging over the land.
medium.q: Why is Egypt described as a rising and raging flood?

medium.explanation: The word describes soldiers who use shields and bows.
medium.q: In the passage, what does "handle" mean in "handle the shield" and "handle and bend the bow"?

answers: It is called to charge but is finally defeated
It refuses to fight and is saved
medium.explanation: The army advances boldly but ultimately falls and is disgraced.
medium.q: How is Egypt's army connected to the outcome of the battle?

answers: A sense of overwhelming power that seems impossible to stop
A picture of weakness and stillness
Proof that Egypt lived beside the sea
challenge.explanation: The image presents Egypt as powerful, though that power cannot save it.
challenge.q: What effect does the comparison between Egypt and raging rivers create?

answers: A day when the sword judges and punishes God's adversaries
A day when the war stops
challenge.explanation: It is a day of judgment in which the sword devours their blood.
challenge.q: What does "a day of vengeance" mean in this context?

answers: The battle is presented as an event of judgment under the Lord's control
The battle is presented as an army celebration
The verse cancels the description of defeat
challenge.explanation: The battle is portrayed as part of the Lord's judgment on His adversaries.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between the sacrifice to the Lord and the description of the battle?

easy.explanation: The prophecy says that Nebuchadrezzar would come against Egypt.
easy.q: Who would come to smite the land of Egypt?

easy.explanation: These three Egyptian places are named in the warning.
easy.q: Which Egyptian cities were told to publish the warning?

easy.explanation: The cities were told to stand fast and prepare because the sword was near.
easy.q: What was Egypt commanded to do?

answers: Because the sword would devour all around it
Because it was about to celebrate victory
medium.explanation: The warning says that the sword would devour round about Egypt.
medium.q: Why was Egypt required to prepare?

medium.explanation: The passage says that the Lord drove them and they could not stand.
medium.q: What caused the downfall of Egypt's valiant men?

answers: Prepare to be taken into captivity
medium.explanation: Egypt is warned to prepare for exile.
medium.q: What does "furnish thyself to go into captivity" mean?

answers: The warning reached different regions of Egypt
The warning concerned only one army
The warning was addressed only to Israel
challenge.explanation: Several cities are named, showing that the warning was broad.
challenge.q: What does the call to several cities show about the scope of the warning?

answers: Defeat leads them to want to return to their own people and land
Defeat leads them to begin a new attack
Defeat proves that the army won
challenge.explanation: The fallen soldiers want to escape the oppressing sword and return home.
challenge.q: What is the connection between the army's fall and the words "Arise, and let us go again"?

answers: The certainty and prominence of his coming
A promise that Egypt will escape
challenge.explanation: The comparison emphasizes that his coming will be certain and unmistakable.
challenge.q: What does the comparison with Tabor and Carmel express about the king's coming?

paragraphs.title: Egypt's Destruction and the Flight of the Mercenaries

easy.explanation: Egypt is called a very fair heifer.
easy.q: What is Egypt compared to at the beginning of this passage?

easy.explanation: The hired men fled together when calamity came.
easy.q: What did Egypt's hired men do?

easy.explanation: They come with axes like men cutting down a forest.
easy.q: What are the numerous enemies compared to?

answers: Its beauty will not prevent the enemy's destruction
medium.explanation: Although Egypt is beautiful, destruction is coming from the north.
medium.q: What does the image of the fair heifer suggest about Egypt's fate?

medium.explanation: The hired men are mercenary soldiers serving Egypt.
medium.q: What does "her hired men" refer to?

answers: To show the extent of the destruction and the enemy's strength
To show that the enemy is retreating
medium.explanation: The image emphasizes the enemy's power and overwhelming numbers.
medium.q: Why is the enemy described as cutting down a forest?

answers: Its countless numbers and comparison to grasshoppers and woodcutters
Its dependence on Egypt's hired men
challenge.explanation: The enemy is innumerable and advances with great destructive force.
challenge.q: What strengthens the impression of the enemy's superiority?

answers: Egypt's voice is heard like a serpent while the enemy advances with axes
challenge.explanation: Egypt cries out, but the enemy continues its forceful advance.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between Egypt's voice and the enemy's advance?

answers: Egypt was defeated and handed over to a northern enemy
Egypt made a treaty with the north
challenge.explanation: The statement summarizes Egypt's defeat and humiliation.
challenge.q: What does the ending, "delivered into the hand of the people of the north," mean?

paragraphs.title: Judgment on Egypt and the Promise of Restoration

answers: No, Pharaoh, Egypt, and those who trust in him
easy.explanation: The passage lists No, Pharaoh, Egypt, and all who trust in him.
easy.q: Whom did the Lord say He would punish?

answers: Into the hand of those who seek its life and Nebuchadrezzar and his servants
Into the hand of the king of Israel
Into the hand of its hired men
easy.explanation: Egypt would be delivered to its enemies and to Babylon's king and servants.
easy.q: Into whose hand would Egypt be delivered?

answers: It would be inhabited as in the days of old
easy.explanation: The Lord promises that Egypt would later be inhabited as in ancient days.
easy.q: What would happen to Egypt afterward?

answers: They are all included in the judgment
They all go into exile with Israel
medium.explanation: The passage includes each of them among those whom the Lord will punish.
medium.q: What do Pharaoh, Egypt, and those who trust in him have in common?

medium.explanation: Here, punishment refers to the Lord's judgment against them.
medium.q: What does "punish" mean in this context?

answers: Judgment and delivery to enemies are followed by the possibility of restoration
Both verses discuss only Egypt's army
medium.explanation: The passage joins severe judgment with a later promise of renewed habitation.
medium.q: How do the two verses relate to each other?

answers: The punishment is not described as everlasting destruction
challenge.explanation: The future promise shows that Egypt's judgment is not permanent annihilation.
challenge.q: What does the promise that Egypt will be inhabited as in the days of old teach about its punishment?

answers: Immediate judgment alongside the possibility of future restoration
challenge.explanation: The verses combine a coming punishment with a later restoration.
challenge.q: What is the central tension in this passage?

answers: To include in the judgment those who rely on Egypt's power
To describe only the mercenary soldiers
challenge.explanation: The judgment extends to those who place their confidence in Egypt.
challenge.q: Why are those who trust in Egypt mentioned with Pharaoh and Egypt?

paragraphs.title: Consolation for Israel Amid the Upheaval of Nations

easy.explanation: The Lord addresses His servant Jacob and Israel.
easy.q: To whom was the command not to fear given?

answers: From afar and from the land of captivity
Only from the battle at Carchemish
easy.explanation: The Lord promises to save Jacob from afar and his seed from captivity.
easy.q: From where did the Lord promise to save Israel?

answers: He would not make Israel a full end
He would not correct Israel at all
He would not bring Israel back
easy.explanation: The Lord says He will not make a full end of Jacob.
easy.q: What would the Lord not do to Israel?

answers: He would be in rest and at ease, and none would make him afraid
medium.explanation: The passage promises Jacob rest, ease, and freedom from fear.
medium.q: What would Jacob's condition be after returning?

answers: Do not be frightened or discouraged
medium.explanation: The command tells Israel not to lose courage through fear.

answers: The nations will be made a full end of, but Israel will not
Israel will be destroyed while the nations are saved
There is no distinction between them
medium.explanation: The Lord promises not to make a full end of Israel.
medium.q: How does the passage distinguish Israel from the nations?

answers: Amid judgment on the nations, Israel receives a promise of protection and return
The message to Israel cancels the judgment on Egypt
challenge.explanation: The conclusion shifts from judgment on Egypt to comfort for Israel.
challenge.q: How does the message to Israel fit with the prophecy of judgment on Egypt?

answers: Israel will be disciplined but not destroyed
Israel will not be punished at all
Israel will be destroyed like the nations
challenge.explanation: The Lord combines discipline with a promise that Israel will not be utterly destroyed.
challenge.q: What does the statement "I will correct thee in measure; yet will I not leave thee wholly unpunished" teach?

answers: Encouragement and the promise of the Lord's presence
A command for Israel to begin a war
challenge.explanation: The repetition strengthens the assurance that the Lord is with Israel.
challenge.q: What is emphasized by the repeated command "Fear thou not"?
